## What this notebook is, and how the manuscript now stands

Both reviewers flagged the construct-validity SEM: overall fit below
conventional thresholds, and very high correlations among Reasoning, Executive
Function and Language. Checks 1--6 below test whether those two problems could
be statistical artifacts — of model size, sample size, IRT measurement error,
pooling across sites, or the missingness pattern. They are not: the misfit and
the high correlations are real features of these data.

That conclusion is what shapes the manuscript's current treatment:

- **Factor structure is reported but not interpreted.** The manuscript gives
  the inter-factor correlations descriptively and defers the question of what
  they mean, because those results are reserved for a dedicated paper in
  preparation. The bifactor / Schmid-Leiman appendix and the factor-count
  comparison table were removed for that reason. `_09-bifactor.qmd` is still in
  the repo and still runs, and `ms.qmd` carries a commented block showing how
  to restore the appendix.
- **The external-validity models changed as a result of the last section of
  this notebook.** Figures 7 and 8 now show the measurement model without age
  (spec A), and Table 8 reports loadings with and without an age control
  (spec A versus spec C). The earlier `factor ~ age` specification (spec B) was
  dropped.

Everything here re-runs the manuscript's own chunks rather than a stand-in
copy, so the numbers are the paper's own and stay in sync when `_08-sem.qmd`
changes.
:::

## Rebuilding the manuscript's models {.unlisted}

### Locating the sibling repositories {.unlisted}

`ms.qmd` sets `levante_dir <- here("../..")` and reads scores from
`levante-pilots`. This notebook resolves that location rather than hardcoding
the offset, testing `../..` first so it matches `ms.qmd` where that layout
holds.

`ms.qmd` also sources `levante-data-meta/plot_settings.R`, which sets ggplot
themes and palettes only. No chunk used here produces a figure that depends on
it, so it is sourced if present and skipped otherwise.

```{r locate-levante-dir}
#| cache: false

find_levante_dir <- function() {
  candidates <- c(here("../.."), here(".."))
  has_pilots <- dir.exists(file.path(candidates, "levante-pilots"))
  if (!any(has_pilots)) {
    stop(glue(
      "Could not find `levante-pilots`.\nLooked in:\n",
      paste0("  - ", normalizePath(candidates, mustWork = FALSE), collapse = "\n"),
      "\n\nThis notebook reruns the real models from _08-sem.qmd, so it needs ",
      "the same scores `ms.qmd` reads. Clone levante-pilots next to this repo ",
      "(or next to its parent) and re-render."
    ), call. = FALSE)
  }
  normalizePath(candidates[has_pilots][1])
}

levante_dir <- find_levante_dir()

### Borrowing the real chunks {.unlisted}

`read_qmd_chunks()` extracts named chunks from a `.qmd` verbatim. The models
below are therefore the manuscript's own specifications, and track subsequent
edits to `_08-sem.qmd` rather than diverging from them.

```{r chunk-reader}
#| cache: false

read_qmd_chunks <- function(path, labels) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE)
  opens <- grep("^```\\{r[ ,}]", lines)
  closes <- grep("^```[[:space:]]*$", lines)

  found <- map(opens, function(open) {
    close <- closes[closes > open]
    if (!length(close)) {
      stop(glue("Unterminated chunk at {basename(path)}:{open}"), call. = FALSE)
    }
    close <- close[1]
    header <- lines[open]
    # label from either ```{r my-label, ...} or a #| label: my-label option line
    label <- str_match(header, "^```\\{r[ ]+([^,}[:space:]]+)")[, 2]
    body <- if (close > open + 1) lines[(open + 1):(close - 1)] else character(0)
    if (is.na(label)) {
      label <- str_match(body, "^#\\|\\s*label:\\s*(\\S+)")[, 2] |>
        discard(is.na) |>
        first()
    }
    list(label = label, body = body)
  })

  available <- map_chr(found, \(c) c$label %||% NA_character_)
  unknown <- setdiff(labels, available)
  if (length(unknown)) {
    stop(glue(
      "Chunk(s) {paste(sQuote(unknown), collapse = ', ')} not found in ",
      "{basename(path)}. Available: {paste(sQuote(na.omit(available)), collapse = ', ')}.\n",
      "The upstream file was probably restructured -- update the chunk list ",
      "in this notebook to match."
    ), call. = FALSE)
  }

  found[match(labels, available)]
}

run_qmd_chunks <- function(path, labels, envir = globalenv()) {
  for (chunk in read_qmd_chunks(path, labels)) {
    eval(parse(text = paste(chunk$body, collapse = "\n")), envir = envir)
  }
  invisible(labels)
}
```

```{r rebuild-models}
#| cache: false

run_qmd_chunks(here("_01-tasks.qmd"),  "task-info")

# sem-g-age     -> model_cov_age, fit_cov_age   (the Figure 6 model)

glue("wide_scores: {nrow(wide_scores)} rows x {ncol(wide_scores)} cols")

### The two models under discussion {.unlisted}

The two reported problems attach to different fitted objects:

- **Overall misfit (CFI, RMSEA): `fit_cov_age`.** The model shown in Figure 6
  (`fig-semplot-core-tasks`): three first-order factors, Stories as an observed
  endogenous outcome, Math as a single-indicator latent whose residual is fixed
  at 1 - rxx, and age predicting each factor and outcome. Identified with
  `std.lv = TRUE`. The CFI and RMSEA quoted in the manuscript come from this
  fit. (When these checks were first run, Math was also an observed outcome and
  the model used marker-variable identification. Both changes are
  reparameterisations or affect one fixed residual only; df, CFI and RMSEA are
  unchanged, so the checks below still apply.)
- **Factor correlations: `fit_3f`.** A three-factor model that treats Math and
  Stories as indicators of Reasoning and Language. It is no longer reported in
  the manuscript -- the factor-count table that once showed it was removed --
  but it is still built in `_08-sem.qmd` because `_10-subsample-robustness.qmd`
  refits it, and `_09-bifactor.qmd` needs it if that appendix is restored.

Checks 1, 2 and 5 target `fit_cov_age`; Checks 3, 4 and 6 target `fit_3f`.

```{r fit-measures-helper}
#| cache: false

grab_measures <- function(fit, label) {
  m <- fitMeasures(fit)
  pick <- function(nm) if (nm %in% names(m)) unname(m[[nm]]) else NA_real_
  tibble(
    model        = label,
    n            = pick("ntotal"),
    npar         = pick("npar"),
    df           = pick("df"),
    chisq        = pick("chisq"),
    chisq_p      = pick("pvalue"),
    cfi          = pick("cfi"),
    cfi_scaled   = pick("cfi.scaled"),
    tli          = pick("tli"),
    rmsea        = pick("rmsea"),
    rmsea_scaled = pick("rmsea.scaled"),
    rmsea_lo     = pick("rmsea.ci.lower"),
    rmsea_hi     = pick("rmsea.ci.upper"),
    rmsea_pclose = pick("rmsea.pvalue"),
    srmr         = pick("srmr"),
    chisq_scaled = pick("chisq.scaled"),
    cfi_robust   = pick("cfi.robust"),
    rmsea_robust = pick("rmsea.robust")
  )
}
```

```{r fit-summaries}
real_fits <- bind_rows(
  grab_measures(fit_cov_age, "fit_cov_age (Figure 6)"),
  grab_measures(fit_3f,      "fit_3f (Table: alt models)")
)

real_fits |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

Both models are estimated with `MLR`, so `lavaan` reports naive, scaled and
robust variants of each index. The manuscript quotes the naive values, and the
simulations below calibrate against those. The scaled values are the
conventional choice under MLR; here they differ negligibly from the naive ones.
The robust RMSEA is substantially larger than both, which is a known
sensitivity of that statistic under FIML with extensive missing data (see
Check 5) and is not interpreted here.

```{r key-numbers}
fig6 <- real_fits |> filter(str_starts(model, "fit_cov_age"))
f3   <- real_fits |> filter(str_starts(model, "fit_3f"))

N_REAL  <- fig6$n
DF_REAL <- fig6$df

glue(
  "Figure 6 model: N = {N_REAL}, df = {DF_REAL}, ",
  "chi-square = {round(fig6$chisq, 1)} (p = {format.pval(fig6$chisq_p, digits = 3)}), ",
  "CFI = {round(fig6$cfi, 3)}, RMSEA = {round(fig6$rmsea, 3)} ",
  "[{round(fig6$rmsea_lo, 3)}, {round(fig6$rmsea_hi, 3)}]"
)
```

## Simulation machinery {.unlisted}

`refit_like()` re-estimates a model on new data using the original `lavaan`
call, so estimator, missing-data handling, identification and optimizer
settings are identical between the observed and simulated fits.

```{r sim-helpers}
#| cache: false

# Re-estimate `fit`'s model on `newdata`, reusing its original lavaan call.
refit_like <- function(fit, newdata, ...) {
  cl <- fit@call
  cl[["data"]] <- quote(.newdata)
  overrides <- list(...)
  for (nm in names(overrides)) cl[[nm]] <- overrides[[nm]]
  .newdata <- newdata
  eval(cl, envir = environment())
}

# lavInspect(.., "converged") only tells us the optimizer stopped. Small or
# unlucky samples can stop at an inadmissible solution (negative residual
# variances, |r| > 1), which should count as a failure, not a datapoint.
# Same criterion _10-subsample-robustness.qmd uses.
# lavaan emits a warning when post.check fails; we are deliberately testing for
# that, so suppress the warning here and account for the discards instead.
fit_is_proper <- function(fit) {
  isTRUE(lavInspect(fit, "converged")) &&
    isTRUE(suppressWarnings(lavInspect(fit, "post.check")))
}

# Observed-variable data actually used by a fit, as a data frame (NAs intact).
model_data <- function(fit) {
  as.data.frame(lavInspect(fit, "data"))
}
```

`simulate_null()` draws samples from a population in which the fitted model
holds exactly, then refits. Population moments are the fitted model's own
implied mean and covariance, so population parameter values equal the
manuscript's estimates. Any misfit in the resulting samples reflects sampling
variation alone, at the observed df and N.

```{r simulate-null}
#| cache: false

# Draw from the model-implied moments of `fit` (where the model holds exactly),
# refit, and return the fit indices. `impose_missing` copies the real
# missingness pattern onto the simulated data by resampling rows of the real
# data's NA mask, so simulated samples carry the same information loss the
# real FIML fit does -- without it, simulated N is effectively larger than real
# N and the null would be optimistic.
simulate_null <- function(fit, n_reps, n_obs = NULL, impose_missing = TRUE,
                          seed = SEED, label = "") {
  base <- refit_like(fit, model_data(fit), fixed.x = FALSE)

  # fixed.x = FALSE makes exogenous variables (age_c) part of the modelled
  # moments so the implied covariance covers every observed variable. It adds
  # parameters and moments in equal number, so df and chi-square are untouched.
  stopifnot(
    all.equal(fitMeasures(base)[["df"]],    fitMeasures(fit)[["df"]]),
    isTRUE(all.equal(fitMeasures(base)[["chisq"]], fitMeasures(fit)[["chisq"]],
                     tolerance = 1e-4))
  )

  implied <- lavInspect(base, "implied")
  Sigma <- as.matrix(implied$cov)
  mu <- if (!is.null(implied$mean)) as.numeric(implied$mean) else rep(0, ncol(Sigma))
  vars <- colnames(Sigma)

  template <- model_data(base)[, vars, drop = FALSE]
  if (is.null(n_obs)) n_obs <- nrow(template)

  stopifnot(setequal(vars, colnames(template)))

  set.seed(seed)
  reps <- map(seq_len(n_reps), function(i) {
    sim <- mvrnorm(n_obs, mu = mu, Sigma = Sigma)
    colnames(sim) <- vars
    sim <- as.data.frame(sim)

    if (impose_missing) {
      rows <- sample(nrow(template), n_obs, replace = TRUE)
      sim[is.na(template[rows, , drop = FALSE])] <- NA_real_
    }

    fit_i <- tryCatch(refit_like(base, sim, fixed.x = FALSE),
                      error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(fit_i) || !fit_is_proper(fit_i)) return(NULL)
    grab_measures(fit_i, label) |> mutate(rep = i, n_obs = n_obs)
  })

  n_ok <- sum(!map_lgl(reps, is.null))
  if (n_ok < n_reps * 0.9) {
    warning(glue(
      "{label}: only {n_ok} of {n_reps} replicates produced a proper solution ",
      "at n = {n_obs}. Treat the summary below as provisional."
    ))
  }

  reps |> compact() |> bind_rows() |> mutate(n_attempted = n_reps, n_proper = n_ok)
}
```

:::

## Check 1 — Is the RMSEA inflated because the model has few df?

Kenny, Kaniskan and McCoach (2015, *Sociological Methods & Research*) show
that RMSEA is upwardly biased and unstable when df is small, and recommend
against reporting it below approximately df = 5. This check establishes whether
the present model falls in that regime.

```{r check1-df}
glue("Figure 6 model df = {DF_REAL}")
```

```{r check1-sim}
#| dependson: [simulate-null, rebuild-models]

null_fig6 <- simulate_null(
  fit_cov_age, n_reps = N_REPS_NULL, seed = SEED,
  label = "fit_cov_age null"
)

null_summary <- function(sims) {
  sims |>
    summarise(
      across(
        c(chisq, cfi, rmsea, srmr),
        list(
          mean = \(x) mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
          median = \(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
          q95 = \(x) quantile(x, .95, na.rm = TRUE),
          q99 = \(x) quantile(x, .99, na.rm = TRUE),
          max = \(x) max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
        ),
        .names = "{.col}__{.fn}"
      ),
      n_proper = first(n_proper), n_attempted = first(n_attempted)
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(contains("__"), names_to = c("index", "stat"), names_sep = "__") |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = value)
}

null_summary(null_fig6) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

Position of the observed values within the null distribution:

```{r check1-percentile}
pctile <- function(sims, index, observed) {
  mean(sims[[index]] >= observed, na.rm = TRUE)
}

tibble(
  index = c("rmsea", "cfi", "chisq"),
  observed = c(fig6$rmsea, fig6$cfi, fig6$chisq),
  null_median = c(median(null_fig6$rmsea), median(null_fig6$cfi), median(null_fig6$chisq)),
  p_null_as_extreme = c(
    pctile(null_fig6, "rmsea", fig6$rmsea),
    mean(null_fig6$cfi <= fig6$cfi, na.rm = TRUE),   # CFI: worse means lower
    pctile(null_fig6, "chisq", fig6$chisq)
  )
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

**Comparison against a generic population.** An earlier version of this check
simulated from stylised parameter values (loadings .7, factor correlations .5)
rather than from the fitted estimates. That variant is retained below, with the
measurement structure read from the `fit_3f` parameter table.

```{r check1-ordinary}
#| dependson: rebuild-models

ordinary_population <- function(fit, loading = .7, factor_r = .5) {
  pe <- parameterEstimates(fit)
  loadings <- pe |> filter(op == "=~") |> dplyr::select(factor = lhs, indicator = rhs)
  factors <- unique(loadings$factor)
  indicators <- unique(loadings$indicator)

  Lambda <- matrix(0, length(indicators), length(factors),
                   dimnames = list(indicators, factors))
  Lambda[cbind(loadings$indicator, loadings$factor)] <- loading

  Phi <- matrix(factor_r, length(factors), length(factors),
                dimnames = list(factors, factors))
  diag(Phi) <- 1

  Sigma <- Lambda %*% Phi %*% t(Lambda)
  diag(Sigma) <- 1  # standardised indicators: residual variance makes up the rest
  list(Sigma = Sigma, indicators = indicators, factors = factors,
       syntax = paste(
         map_chr(factors, \(f) {
           ind <- loadings$indicator[loadings$factor == f]
           glue("{f} =~ {paste(ind, collapse = ' + ')}")
         }),
         collapse = "\n"
       ))
}

pop <- ordinary_population(fit_3f)

set.seed(SEED)
ordinary_null <- map(seq_len(N_REPS_NULL), function(i) {
  sim <- as.data.frame(mvrnorm(N_REAL, mu = rep(0, nrow(pop$Sigma)), Sigma = pop$Sigma))
  fit_i <- tryCatch(
    cfa(pop$syntax, data = sim, estimator = "MLR", std.lv = TRUE),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(fit_i) || !fit_is_proper(fit_i)) return(NULL)
  grab_measures(fit_i, "ordinary-values null")
}) |>
  compact() |>
  bind_rows()

glue(
  "Measurement-only structure from fit_3f: df = {ordinary_null$df[1]}, ",
  "simulated at N = {N_REAL}.\n",
  "RMSEA null: median {round(median(ordinary_null$rmsea), 4)}, ",
  "95th pct {round(quantile(ordinary_null$rmsea, .95), 4)}, ",
  "max {round(max(ordinary_null$rmsea), 4)}."
)
```

This variant omits the age regressions, so its df differs from that of the
Figure 6 model. It is included only to confirm agreement with the
real-estimates null, which is the result to cite.

## Check 2 — Is the significant chi-square just large N?

The chi-square test is consistent: for fixed misspecification its expected
value grows approximately linearly in N, so at N ≈ `r format(round(N_REAL))`
rejection is near-certain. This check establishes whether sample size also
accounts for CFI and RMSEA, which are constructed to be less N-dependent.

The sample-size-free summary of misfit is the fit function value
$F_{ML} \approx \chi^2/(N-1)$, of which RMSEA is a df-scaled transformation:

```{r check2-fml}
tibble(
  model = real_fits$model,
  n = real_fits$n,
  df = real_fits$df,
  chisq = real_fits$chisq,
  F_ML = real_fits$chisq / (real_fits$n - 1),
  rmsea_from_F = sqrt(pmax(0, (real_fits$chisq / (real_fits$n - 1)) / real_fits$df -
                             1 / (real_fits$n - 1))),
  rmsea_reported = real_fits$rmsea
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

```{r check2-sweep}
#| dependson: [simulate-null, rebuild-models]

n_grid <- sort(unique(c(N_SWEEP_EXTRA, N_REAL)))

null_by_n <- map(n_grid, function(n) {
  simulate_null(
    fit_cov_age, n_reps = N_REPS_NULL, n_obs = n,
    seed = SEED + n, label = glue("null n = {n}")
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows()

null_by_n |>
  summarise(
    chisq_median = median(chisq),
    chisq_p_sig = mean(chisq_p < .05),
    cfi_median = median(cfi),
    rmsea_median = median(rmsea),
    rmsea_q95 = quantile(rmsea, .95),
    .by = n_obs
  ) |>
  arrange(n_obs) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

Under correct specification, chi-square tracks df rather than N, rejection
rates remain near the nominal .05 at every N, and RMSEA remains near zero
throughout, including at the observed N. Sample size does not produce the
observed RMSEA of `r round(fig6$rmsea, 3)`.

```{r check2-plot}
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3

null_by_n |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(n_obs), rmsea)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = .15, width = .5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = fig6$rmsea, colour = "firebrick", linetype = 2) +
  labs(
    x = "Simulated N", y = "RMSEA",
    title = "RMSEA under a correctly specified model, by sample size",
    subtitle = glue("Dashed line = observed RMSEA ({round(fig6$rmsea, 3)}) in the Figure 6 model")
  )
```

## Check 3 — Do IRT theta measurement errors inflate the factor correlations?

Each indicator is an IRT ability estimate carrying measurement error. The
concern is that ignoring this error distorts the latent correlations. Random,
mutually uncorrelated measurement error is absorbed by CFA residual variances,
so latent correlations should already be disattenuated. This check tests that
on the fitted structure.

### Real marginal reliabilities

Reliabilities are taken from the `load-rxx` chunk of `_06-reliability.qmd`
(the source of Table 6) and averaged across the groups reported there.

```{r check3-rxx}
#| dependson: rebuild-models

# load-rxx blanks repeated task/itemtype/invariance labels for display;
# undo that so the table can be joined on.
task_rxx_clean <- task_rxx |>
  mutate(across(c(task, itemtype, invariance), \(x) na_if(as.character(x), ""))) |>
  fill(task, itemtype, invariance, .direction = "down")

rxx_by_task <- task_rxx_clean |>
  summarise(rxx = mean(empirical_rxx, na.rm = TRUE), n_groups = n(), .by = task) |>
  left_join(task_info |> distinct(item_task, task) |> mutate(task = as.character(task)),
            by = "task") |>
  filter(!is.na(item_task))

rxx_by_task |> mutate(rxx = round(rxx, 3)) |> arrange(item_task)
```

### Simulating theta error on the real `fit_3f` structure

True factors are generated at a specified correlation; indicators are
generated using the standardised loadings from `fit_3f`; each indicator then
receives independent noise scaled so that its reliability equals that task's
marginal reliability. Measurement-error inflation would appear as recovered
correlations systematically above the population value.

```{r check3-sim}
#| dependson: [check3-rxx, sim-helpers]

structure_3f <- parameterEstimates(fit_3f, standardized = TRUE) |>
  filter(op == "=~") |>
  dplyr::select(factor = lhs, item_task = rhs, lambda = std.all)

measurement_syntax <- structure_3f |>
  summarise(rhs = paste(item_task, collapse = " + "), .by = factor) |>
  glue_data("{factor} =~ {rhs}") |>
  paste(collapse = "\n")

cat(measurement_syntax, "\n")

sim_spec <- structure_3f |>
  left_join(rxx_by_task |> dplyr::select(item_task, rxx), by = "item_task")

missing_rxx <- sim_spec |> filter(is.na(rxx)) |> pull(item_task)
if (length(missing_rxx)) {
  stop(glue(
    "No marginal reliability found for: {paste(missing_rxx, collapse = ', ')}. ",
    "These indicators appear in fit_3f but not in the Table 6 reliability output."
  ), call. = FALSE)
}

simulate_measurement_error <- function(spec, r_pop, n_obs, n_reps, seed) {
  factors <- unique(spec$factor)
  Phi <- matrix(r_pop, length(factors), length(factors),
                dimnames = list(factors, factors))
  diag(Phi) <- 1

  set.seed(seed)
  reps <- map(seq_len(n_reps), function(i) {
    F_true <- mvrnorm(n_obs, mu = rep(0, length(factors)), Sigma = Phi)
    colnames(F_true) <- factors

    obs <- map(seq_len(nrow(spec)), function(j) {
      lambda <- spec$lambda[j]
      rxx <- spec$rxx[j]
      # true task score: unit variance, lambda on its factor
      tau <- lambda * F_true[, spec$factor[j]] +
        rnorm(n_obs, sd = sqrt(max(0, 1 - lambda^2)))
      # theta error variance chosen so var(tau) / var(tau + e) == rxx
      tau + rnorm(n_obs, sd = sqrt((1 - rxx) / rxx))
    }) |>
      set_names(spec$item_task) |>
      as.data.frame()

    fit_i <- tryCatch(
      cfa(measurement_syntax, data = obs, estimator = "ML", std.lv = TRUE),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    if (is.null(fit_i) || !fit_is_proper(fit_i)) return(NULL)

    parameterEstimates(fit_i, standardized = TRUE) |>
      filter(op == "~~", lhs != rhs, lhs %in% factors, rhs %in% factors) |>
      transmute(pair = paste(lhs, rhs, sep = "-"), r_hat = std.all,
                r_pop = r_pop, rep = i)
  })

  n_ok <- sum(!map_lgl(reps, is.null))
  # Discarded replicates are not missing at random -- inadmissible solutions
  # cluster where the population correlation approaches 1 -- so a high discard
  # rate would itself bias the recovered mean. Surface it rather than hide it.
  if (n_ok < n_reps * 0.9) {
    warning(glue(
      "r_pop = {r_pop}: only {n_ok} of {n_reps} replicates gave a proper ",
      "solution. The recovered correlation for this condition is conditioned ",
      "on admissibility and should be read with that in mind."
    ))
  }

  reps |> compact() |> bind_rows() |>
    mutate(n_proper = n_ok, n_attempted = n_reps)
}

r_pop_grid <- c(.30, .50, .70, .85, .98)

me_results <- map(seq_along(r_pop_grid), function(k) {
  simulate_measurement_error(
    sim_spec, r_pop = r_pop_grid[k], n_obs = N_REAL,
    n_reps = N_REPS_ME, seed = SEED + 1000 * k
  )
}) |>
  bind_rows()

me_summary <- me_results |>
  summarise(
    r_hat_mean = mean(r_hat), r_hat_sd = sd(r_hat),
    bias = mean(r_hat) - first(r_pop),
    n_proper = first(n_proper), n_attempted = first(n_attempted),
    .by = c(r_pop, pair)
  ) |>
  arrange(r_pop, pair)

me_summary |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

```{r check3-plot}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4

me_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(r_pop, r_hat_mean, colour = pair)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Population factor correlation", y = "Recovered factor correlation",
    colour = NULL,
    title = "Latent correlations under realistic IRT theta error",
    subtitle = "Dashed line = unbiased recovery"
  )
```

Observed correlations, for comparison:

```{r check3-observed}
parameterEstimates(fit_3f, standardized = TRUE) |>
  filter(op == "~~", lhs != rhs, lhs %in% c("reasoning", "ef", "language"),
         rhs %in% c("reasoning", "ef", "language")) |>
  transmute(pair = paste(lhs, rhs, sep = "-"), r = round(std.all, 3))
```

The `n_proper` and `n_attempted` columns should be inspected before
interpreting any row. Inadmissible solutions concentrate in the highest
condition: a population correlation near .98 leaves the factors nearly
collinear and a substantial share of replicates fail `post.check`, while
conditions from .30 to .85 converge cleanly. This parallels the Heywood
behaviour reported in `_09-bifactor.qmd` for the direct bifactor model. Because
discarded replicates are conditioned on admissibility, the recovered mean in a
high-discard condition is not an unbiased estimate of bias.

Measurement-error inflation would place the simulated points above the
diagonal, most visibly at low population correlations. The relevant quantities
are the `bias` column and the distance from the dashed line.

## Check 4 — Does pooling across sites manufacture the correlations?

<!-- The chunks in this section borrow from _10-subsample-robustness.qmd and are
cached, because they refit the model on 200 subsamples. knitr keys the cache on
each chunk's own code, so edits to _10-subsample-robustness.qmd will NOT
invalidate them: clear sem/fit_diagnostics_cache/ by hand if that file
changes. -->

This analysis is George's, reported in the manuscript as appendix
`#apx-subsample` (`_10-subsample-robustness.qmd`). It is reproduced here for
completeness, so that all six checks can be read together. The code below is
borrowed from that file verbatim by `read_qmd_chunks()` rather than
reimplemented, so these results are his analysis rather than a reconstruction
of it.

The mechanism at issue: if sites differ in overall ability level, pooling them
induces variance shared by every task. Each task then correlates with every
other partly because scoring well on one indicates which site a child is from,
which predicts scoring well on the rest. Site differences can therefore inflate
all correlations and produce a pattern resembling a general factor. Check 5
shows that site accounts for roughly half of each factor's variance, so this is
a substantial concern rather than a remote one.

Two designs address it. Equal-size-per-site subsampling removes the sample-size
imbalance across sites. Within-site fits eliminate pooling entirely, and are
the decisive test: with no aggregation, there can be no aggregation artifact.

```{r check4-site-ns}
#| dependson: rebuild-models

run_qmd_chunks(here("_10-subsample-robustness.qmd"),
               c("tbl-site-ns", "subsample-functions"))

site_ns |> rename(Site = site_label, N = n)
```

Note that `subsample-functions` redefines `fit_is_proper()`. The definition is
equivalent to the one used elsewhere in this notebook except that it does not
suppress `lavaan`'s warning, so the chunks below emit warnings where a
replicate reaches an inadmissible solution.

```{r check4-subsample}
#| dependson: check4-site-ns
#| cache: true

run_qmd_chunks(here("_10-subsample-robustness.qmd"), "subsample-refit")

full_sample_cors <- extract_cors_3f(fit_3f) |> rename(r_full = r)

subsample_results |>
  summarise(
    r_mean = mean(r), r_sd = sd(r),
    r_q025 = quantile(r, .025), r_q975 = quantile(r, .975),
    .by = pair
  ) |>
  left_join(full_sample_cors, by = "pair") |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r check4-subsample-n}
#| dependson: check4-subsample

glue("{n_distinct(subsample_results$rep)} of {n_reps} replicates reached an ",
     "admissible solution, at n = {min_site_n} per site ",
     "({min_site_n * nrow(site_ns)} total per replicate).")
```

Balancing the sites leaves the full-sample estimates essentially unchanged, so
the imbalance across sites is not responsible for the magnitude of the
correlations.

```{r check4-within-site}
#| dependson: check4-site-ns
#| cache: true

run_qmd_chunks(here("_10-subsample-robustness.qmd"), "within-site-fits")

# within-site-fits drops sites that fail, so refit here retaining every site
# and recording admissibility, since an inadmissible solution is itself
# informative rather than something to omit.
within_site_all <- site_ns |>
  filter(n >= 100) |>
  pull(site_label) |>
  map(function(s) {
    d <- filter(wide_scores, site_label == s)
    f <- tryCatch(fit_3f_on(d), error = function(e) NULL)
    if (is.null(f) || !isTRUE(lavInspect(f, "converged"))) {
      return(tibble(site_label = s, n = nrow(d), note = "did not converge"))
    }
    extract_cors_3f(f) |>
      mutate(site_label = s, n = nrow(d),
             admissible = isTRUE(suppressWarnings(lavInspect(f, "post.check"))))
  }) |>
  bind_rows()

within_site_all |>
  mutate(r = round(r, 3)) |>
  dplyr::select(site_label, n, pair, r, admissible) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = pair, values_from = r) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

### Interpretation

**Pooling does not create the correlations.** Within a single site, where no
aggregation across sites is possible, Reasoning and Executive Function remain
correlated between approximately .86 and .94 in the sites that produce
admissible solutions. Equal-size subsampling likewise leaves the full-sample
values close to unchanged.

**Pooling does inflate them modestly.** The within-site values are lower than
the pooled estimate (.976), by roughly .04 to .12. Aggregation therefore
contributes to the magnitude without accounting for it; a within-site
correlation of .86 remains a substantial discriminant validity problem.

**The two Colombian sites return inadmissible solutions.** The rural site
yields a Reasoning-EF correlation above 1, which is not a possible correlation.
Those rows carry no information about the correlations and should be read only
as evidence that the model is not estimable within those sites, which is
consistent with the coverage figures in Check 5.

**The two methods of adjusting for site do not agree in magnitude.** Fitting
within sites lowers the Reasoning-EF correlation; entering site as a covariate
(Check 6) raises it. Site-as-covariate removes site differences in factor means
while imposing a common covariance structure across sites, whereas within-site
fits allow all parameters to differ. That the two diverge is further evidence of
the between-site heterogeneity identified in Check 5, and indicates that
"adjusting for site" is not a single well-defined operation for these data. The
within-site result makes fewer assumptions and is the one to report; the
direction of the conclusion is the same under both.

## Check 5 — Does the missingness pattern explain the misfit?

The analysis sample is substantially incomplete. This check tests whether that
accounts for the fit indices. It does not: missingness masks misfit here rather
than producing it.

### How much data each variable actually has

```{r check5-coverage}
#| dependson: rebuild-models

model_vars <- colnames(lavInspect(fit_cov_age, "data"))

# Read each variable's role out of the fitted model rather than hardcoding it.
pe_fig6 <- parameterEstimates(fit_cov_age)
indicator_of <- pe_fig6 |> filter(op == "=~") |> dplyr::select(factor = lhs, var = rhs)
exogenous <- setdiff(pe_fig6$rhs[pe_fig6$op == "~"], c(indicator_of$var, ""))

coverage <- tibble(var = model_vars) |>
  left_join(indicator_of, by = "var") |>
  mutate(
    role = case_when(
      !is.na(factor) ~ paste(factor, "indicator"),
      var %in% exogenous ~ "exogenous predictor",
      TRUE ~ "observed outcome"
    ),
    n_obs = map_int(var, \(v) sum(!is.na(wide_scores[[v]]))),
    pct_missing = map_dbl(var, \(v) 100 * mean(is.na(wide_scores[[v]])))
  ) |>
  dplyr::select(var, role, n_obs, pct_missing) |>
  arrange(pct_missing)

coverage |> mutate(pct_missing = round(pct_missing, 1))
```

```{r check5-coverage-counts}
#| dependson: check5-coverage

task_vars <- setdiff(model_vars, exogenous)
k_task <- rowSums(!is.na(wide_scores[, task_vars, drop = FALSE]))

glue(
  "Of the {length(task_vars)} task scores, the typical child contributes ",
  "mean {round(mean(k_task), 2)} / median {median(k_task)}; ",
  "{sum(k_task == length(task_vars))} children ",
  "({round(100 * mean(k_task == length(task_vars)), 1)}%) have all of them."
)

table(`tasks observed` = k_task)
```

`age_c` is never missing, so including it would overstate coverage. The
figures above cover the task scores only.

### The missingness is structured by site

```{r check5-by-site}
#| dependson: check5-coverage

wide_scores |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    across(all_of(task_vars), \(x) round(100 * mean(is.na(x)))),
    .by = site_label
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n))

wide_scores |>
  mutate(k = rowSums(!is.na(pick(all_of(task_vars))))) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(), mean_tasks = round(mean(k), 2), median_tasks = median(k),
    pct_complete = round(100 * mean(k == length(task_vars)), 1),
    .by = site_label
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(n))
```

Coverage is not distributed evenly across the sample; it approximates a design
variable. The two Colombian sites contribute most of the sample but few tasks
per child, while the German and Canadian sites are substantially denser.

### Refitting where the data are dense

```{r check5-density-fits}
#| dependson: check5-by-site
#| cache: true

fit_fig6_on <- function(data) {
  tryCatch(
    sem(model_cov_age, data = data, estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml",
        std.lv = FALSE, optim.method = "nlminb",
        control = list(iter.max = 50000, rel.tol = 1e-6)),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
}

summarise_subset <- function(data, label) {
  f <- fit_fig6_on(data)
  if (is.null(f) || !lavInspect(f, "converged")) {
    return(tibble(model = label, n = nrow(data), note = "did not converge"))
  }
  grab_measures(f, label) |>
    mutate(proper = isTRUE(suppressWarnings(lavInspect(f, "post.check"))))
}

dense_sites  <- c("mpieva-de", "western-ca")
sparse_sites <- setdiff(unique(as.character(wide_scores$site_label)), dense_sites)

density_fits <- bind_rows(
  summarise_subset(wide_scores, "All pooled"),
  map(sort(unique(as.character(wide_scores$site_label))),
      \(s) summarise_subset(filter(wide_scores, site_label == s), s)) |> bind_rows(),
  summarise_subset(filter(wide_scores, site_label %in% dense_sites), "Dense sites only"),
  summarise_subset(filter(wide_scores, site_label %in% sparse_sites), "Sparse sites only")
)

density_fits |>
  dplyr::select(model, n, df, chisq, cfi, rmsea, srmr, proper) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

**RMSEA and SRMR diverge at the sparse sites.** The Colombian subsets return
RMSEA of approximately .02 to .04 alongside improper solutions, and SRMR of
approximately .21 at the rural site. With roughly 3.5 observed tasks per child
there is little covariance structure available to misfit, so power to detect
misspecification is low and RMSEA is correspondingly small. The `proper` column
should be checked before these rows are interpreted.

**Pooling the two dense sites yields worse fit than either alone** (RMSEA .094
against .067 and .021), and worse than the full sample. This indicates
between-site heterogeneity in covariance structure.

**Missingness does not account for the misfit.** Were it responsible, the
sparse subsets would fit worst and the dense subsets best; the reverse holds.
This agrees with Check 1, in which the null simulation imposes the observed
missingness pattern on correctly specified data and returns RMSEA near zero.

Missingness does affect interpretation. The sample is dominated by sites
contributing little covariance information, and FIML assumes data are missing
at random conditional on the modelled variables. Site is not in this model and
coverage depends strongly on site, so that assumption carries weight here. This
is a limitation of interpretation and generalisability rather than an artifact
accounting for the misfit.

## Check 6 — Are the factors empirically distinguishable?

Checks 1 to 5 test whether the reported values are artifacts. This check tests
what the values imply. Two questions: whether the factor correlations are
distinguishable from unity, and whether they survive adjustment for site.

### Interval estimates and a test against r = 1

Because `fit_3f` is fitted with `std.lv = TRUE`, factor variances are fixed at
1 and each factor covariance is itself the correlation, so `lavaan`'s
confidence intervals apply directly to the correlations.

```{r check6-ci}
#| dependson: rebuild-models

parameterEstimates(fit_3f, standardized = TRUE, ci = TRUE, level = .95) |>
  filter(op == "~~", lhs != rhs,
         lhs %in% c("reasoning", "ef", "language"),
         rhs %in% c("reasoning", "ef", "language")) |>
  transmute(pair = paste(lhs, rhs, sep = "-"),
            r = std.all, se = se,
            ci_lower = ci.lower, ci_upper = ci.upper) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

A correlation statistically indistinguishable from 1 means the two factors are
not separable: a model merging them fits as well as one keeping them apart.
The syntax below is regenerated from the `fit_3f` parameter table so the
constrained and free models are guaranteed nested and identical apart from the
single fixed correlation.

```{r check6-unity}
#| dependson: rebuild-models
#| cache: true

build_3f_syntax <- function(fit, fixed_pair = NULL, fixed_value = 1) {
  pe <- parameterEstimates(fit)
  loads <- pe |> filter(op == "=~") |> dplyr::select(factor = lhs, ind = rhs)
  factors <- unique(loads$factor)
  preds <- setdiff(unique(pe$rhs[pe$op == "~"]), "")

  measurement <- map_chr(factors, \(f)
    glue("{f} =~ {paste(loads$ind[loads$factor == f], collapse = ' + ')}"))
  covariances <- combn(factors, 2, simplify = FALSE) |>
    map_chr(\(pr) if (!is.null(fixed_pair) && setequal(pr, fixed_pair))
      glue("{pr[1]} ~~ {fixed_value}*{pr[2]}") else glue("{pr[1]} ~~ {pr[2]}"))
  regressions <- map_chr(factors, \(f)
    glue("{f} ~ {paste(preds, collapse = ' + ')}"))

  paste(c(measurement, covariances, regressions), collapse = "\n")
}

fit_3f_syntax <- function(syntax) {
  sem(syntax, data = wide_scores, estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml",
      std.lv = TRUE, optim.method = "nlminb",
      control = list(iter.max = 50000, rel.tol = 1e-6))
}

# Free model rebuilt from the parameter table; must reproduce fit_3f exactly.
fit_free <- fit_3f_syntax(build_3f_syntax(fit_3f))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(fitMeasures(fit_free)[["chisq"]],
                           fitMeasures(fit_3f)[["chisq"]], tolerance = 1e-4)))

factor_pairs <- combn(c("reasoning", "ef", "language"), 2, simplify = FALSE)

unity_tests <- map(factor_pairs, function(pr) {
  fit_con <- tryCatch(fit_3f_syntax(build_3f_syntax(fit_3f, pr)),
                      error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(fit_con) || !lavInspect(fit_con, "converged")) {
    return(tibble(pair = paste(pr, collapse = "-"), note = "did not converge"))
  }
  lrt <- suppressWarnings(as.data.frame(lavTestLRT(fit_con, fit_free)))
  row <- lrt[!is.na(lrt[["Chisq diff"]]), ][1, ]
  tibble(
    pair        = paste(pr, collapse = "-"),
    chisq_diff  = row[["Chisq diff"]],
    df_diff     = row[["Df diff"]],
    p_value     = row[["Pr(>Chisq)"]],
    aic_free    = fitMeasures(fit_free)[["aic"]],
    aic_r1      = fitMeasures(fit_con)[["aic"]],
    bic_free    = fitMeasures(fit_free)[["bic"]],
    bic_r1      = fitMeasures(fit_con)[["bic"]],
    proper_r1   = isTRUE(suppressWarnings(lavInspect(fit_con, "post.check")))
  )
}) |> bind_rows()

unity_tests |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

A non-significant `p_value` indicates that fixing the correlation to 1 does
not significantly degrade fit. Lower `aic_r1` / `bic_r1` than `aic_free` /
`bic_free` indicates that the merged model is preferred on information
criteria.

`proper_r1` is `FALSE` for every pair by construction, not as a diagnostic
failure. Fixing one off-diagonal element of a 3 x 3 latent correlation matrix
to 1 makes that matrix singular, so `post.check` necessarily reports a
non-positive-definite latent covariance matrix. This is the intended
constraint rather than an estimation problem, and is the one place in this
notebook where a `FALSE` in a `proper` column should not be treated as grounds
for discarding the result.

### Site as a covariate

An alternative to a multi-group model is to enter site as dummy predictors
alongside age. This removes between-site differences in factor *means*, so the
residual factor correlations are net of site composition. It does not model
between-site differences in covariance structure, which is the heterogeneity
identified in Check 5.

```{r check6-site-covariate}
#| dependson: rebuild-models
#| cache: true

d_site <- wide_scores |> mutate(site_label = fct_drop(site_label))
site_dummies <- model.matrix(~ site_label, data = d_site)[, -1, drop = FALSE]
colnames(site_dummies) <- paste0("site", seq_len(ncol(site_dummies)))
d_site <- bind_cols(d_site, as.data.frame(site_dummies))

reference_site <- levels(d_site$site_label)[1]
site_terms <- paste(colnames(site_dummies), collapse = " + ")

mdl_3f_site <- glue("
reasoning =~ mrot + matrix + math
ef        =~ mg + sds + hf
language  =~ vocab + trog + tom
reasoning ~~ ef + language
ef ~~ language
reasoning ~ age_c + {site_terms}
ef        ~ age_c + {site_terms}
language  ~ age_c + {site_terms}
")

fit_3f_site <- sem(mdl_3f_site, data = d_site, estimator = "MLR",
                   missing = "fiml", std.lv = TRUE, optim.method = "nlminb",
                   control = list(iter.max = 50000, rel.tol = 1e-6))

glue("Reference site: {reference_site}; {ncol(site_dummies)} dummy predictors. ",
     "Proper solution: {isTRUE(suppressWarnings(lavInspect(fit_3f_site, 'post.check')))}")

extract_cors <- function(fit, label) {
  parameterEstimates(fit, standardized = TRUE) |>
    filter(op == "~~", lhs != rhs,
           lhs %in% c("reasoning", "ef", "language"),
           rhs %in% c("reasoning", "ef", "language")) |>
    transmute(pair = paste(lhs, rhs, sep = "-"), !!label := round(std.all, 3))
}

left_join(extract_cors(fit_3f, "age_only"),
          extract_cors(fit_3f_site, "age_plus_site"), by = "pair")
```

```{r check6-site-fit}
#| dependson: check6-site-covariate

bind_rows(grab_measures(fit_3f, "age only"),
          grab_measures(fit_3f_site, "age + site")) |>
  dplyr::select(model, n, df, chisq, cfi, rmsea, srmr) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

round(lavInspect(fit_3f_site, "r2")[c("reasoning", "ef", "language")], 3)
```

The `r2` values give the proportion of each factor's variance attributable to
age and site jointly, indexing how much of the between-person variance is
associated with sampling site.

### Interpretation

Three results follow.

**The failure of discriminant validity is specific to one factor pair.**
Reasoning and Executive Function are not statistically distinguishable: the
confidence interval for their correlation includes 1, constraining it to 1 does
not significantly degrade fit, and both AIC and BIC favour the constrained
model. The other two pairs are clearly distinguishable, with the r = 1
constraint strongly rejected in each case and both information criteria
favouring the free model. Language is therefore separable from both Reasoning
and Executive Function; the three-factor structure fails only in that it does
not separate Reasoning from Executive Function. This is a more precise
statement of the problem than the magnitude of the correlations alone.

**Adjusting for site does not reduce the collinearity.** Site accounts for a
substantial share of factor variance, but the Reasoning-EF correlation
increases rather than decreases once site is partialled out. The collinearity
is therefore within-site, not a product of pooling heterogeneous samples. This
should be read alongside the within-site fits in Check 4, which move the
correlation in the opposite direction. The
Reasoning-Language and EF-Language correlations decrease, indicating that site
composition inflates them: adjusting for site improves Language's separation
from the other two factors rather than reducing it.

**Adjusting for site degrades fit.** Dummy covariates constrain factor means
across sites but impose a common covariance structure, which Check 5 shows does
not hold. The site-covariate specification is therefore informative about the
correlations but is not a remedy for the misfit.

A constraint on interpretation: pairwise coverage for the indicator pairs that
identify the Reasoning-EF distinction is low (see Check 5), and each factor has
three indicators. "Not distinguishable from r = 1" is therefore consistent with
two readings — that the constructs are not separable in this population, or
that these data lack the information to separate them. The present design does
not adjudicate between them.

```{r check6-coverage-crossfactor}
#| dependson: [check6-unity, check5-coverage]

cov_mat <- lavInspect(fit_3f, "coverage")
r_inds  <- c("mrot", "matrix", "math")
e_inds  <- c("mg", "sds", "hf")

glue(
  "Pairwise coverage for Reasoning x EF indicator pairs: ",
  "min {round(min(cov_mat[r_inds, e_inds]), 2)}, ",
  "median {round(median(cov_mat[r_inds, e_inds]), 2)}, ",
  "max {round(max(cov_mat[r_inds, e_inds]), 2)}."
)

round(cov_mat[c(r_inds, e_inds), c(r_inds, e_inds)], 2)
```

## Summary

```{r summary-table}
tibble(
  check = c(
    "1. Low df inflates RMSEA",
    "2. Large N inflates chi-square",
    "3. IRT theta error inflates factor correlations",
    "4. Site pooling manufactures the correlations",
    "5. Missingness drives the misfit",
    "6. Factors are empirically distinguishable"
  ),
  target = c("fit_cov_age", "fit_cov_age", "fit_3f", "fit_3f", "fit_cov_age",
             "fit_3f"),
  evidence = c(
    glue("df = {DF_REAL}; null RMSEA median {round(median(null_fig6$rmsea), 3)}, ",
         "95th pct {round(quantile(null_fig6$rmsea, .95), 3)} vs observed {round(fig6$rmsea, 3)}"),
    glue("Null rejection rate near .05 at every N; null RMSEA ~0 at N = {N_REAL}"),
    glue("Max |bias| across conditions = {round(max(abs(me_summary$bias)), 3)}"),
    glue("Within-site fits (no pooling) still give Reasoning-EF ",
         "{paste(round(range(within_site_all$r[within_site_all$pair == 'reasoning-ef' & within_site_all$admissible], na.rm = TRUE), 2), collapse = '-')}; ",
         "equal-size subsampling leaves full-sample values near unchanged"),
    glue("Runs the other way: sparse sites show better RMSEA but improper ",
         "solutions; dense sites pooled are worse ",
         "({round(density_fits$rmsea[density_fits$model == 'Dense sites only'], 3)}) ",
         "than the full sample ({round(fig6$rmsea, 3)})"),
    glue("Reasoning-EF r = 1 not rejected ",
         "(p = {round(unity_tests$p_value[unity_tests$pair == 'reasoning-ef'], 2)}, ",
         "AIC/BIC favour the constraint); other two pairs clearly separable ",
         "(p < .001); adjusting for site raises Reasoning-EF, not lowers it")
  )
)
```

All values are recomputed at each render from the fitted models.

Checks 1, 2, 3 and 5 test candidate artifacts; none accounts for the reported
misfit or the magnitude of the correlations. Check 4, reproduced from George's
appendix analysis, shows that pooling across sites inflates the correlations
modestly but does not produce them. Check 6 localises the discriminant
validity problem: Reasoning and Executive Function are not statistically
distinguishable, this does not arise from pooling across sites, and the
remaining two factor pairs are clearly separable.

The general-factor account in `_09-bifactor.qmd` (appendix `#apx-bifactor`) is
consistent with these results, subject to the identification constraint noted
in Check 6: with three indicators per factor and low pairwise coverage, the
data cannot distinguish non-separable constructs from insufficient information
to separate them.

Check 5 additionally identifies between-site heterogeneity in covariance
structure as a contributor to the misfit, which is not addressed by the
existing robustness analyses.

## Domain-specific models: EF and Language (exploratory)

The sections above concern the main construct-validity SEM. This section
concerns the two *external-validity* models in `_08-sem.qmd` (`fit_ef` and
`fit_lang`).

**These results have since been adopted in the manuscript.** Figures 7 and 8
now show spec A (the measurement model, no age), and Table 8 reports the spec A
and spec C loadings side by side as an age control. Spec B, which the
manuscript previously used, has been dropped: the age slope it contributed is
developmental-sensitivity evidence already covered by the age-models section,
and it answers a developmental rather than a validity question. The comparison
below is what motivated that change.

### Data note: the MEFS score labels are wrong upstream

The `metric_type` labels in `scores_mefs.rds` do not match what they contain.
Confirmed with Mike (2026-10-09) as a known upstream issue, and consistent with
the MEFS Technical Report (Reflection Sciences, *MEFS Technical Report 2026*,
v. 07.26.26), which documents three
distinct scores: a **Total Score** (0-100, combining trial accuracy and
response time via a proprietary algorithm), a **U.S. National Percentile**
(referenced to same-age-in-months US norms), and a **National Standard Score**
(M = 100, SD = 15).

| Label in the data | Actual score | Evidence in this sample |
|---|---|---|
| `standard_score` | Total Score | climbs with age (+3.6 pts/year, R² = .29), max 94 |
| `total_score` | U.S. National Percentile | flat with age (R² = .007), roughly uniform 0-85 |

The National Standard Score is not present in the data at all. (The manuscript
cites @carlson2021 as the general MEFS reference; the score definitions and
reliability figures used here are from the 2026 edition of the technical
report, which is the version consulted.) The models below
use the Total Score (labelled `standard_score`), which is the appropriate choice
for a model containing age: the percentile is already age-referenced, so its age
variance has been removed, and being a rank transform it is also non-linearly
related to the underlying scale.

```{r domain-mefs-labels}
#| cache: false
# Not cached: this chunk re-runs chunks borrowed from _08-sem.qmd, whose
# contents can change without this chunk's own code changing -- which would
# otherwise leave a stale cache silently reporting a superseded specification.
#| dependson: rebuild-models

run_qmd_chunks(here("_08-sem.qmd"), c("prep-sem-ef", "prep-sem-lang"))

mefs_raw <- read_rds(here(pilots_dir, "02_scoring_outputs/scores/scores_mefs.rds")) |>
  dplyr::select(user_id, age, metric_type, metric_value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = metric_type, values_from = metric_value,
              values_fn = first) |>
  filter(!is.na(age))

# Documents the label problem rather than assuming the reader takes it on trust.
map(c("standard_score", "total_score"), function(v) {
  fit <- lm(mefs_raw[[v]] ~ mefs_raw$age)
  tibble(label = v,
         slope_per_year = coef(fit)[[2]],
         r2_age = summary(fit)$r.squared,
         median = median(mefs_raw[[v]], na.rm = TRUE),
         sd = sd(mefs_raw[[v]], na.rm = TRUE),
         max = max(mefs_raw[[v]], na.rm = TRUE))
}) |> bind_rows() |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r domain-mefs-agebands}
#| dependson: domain-mefs-labels

mefs_raw |>
  mutate(band = cut(age, c(5, 7, 9, 11, 14), right = FALSE,
                    labels = c("5-6", "7-8", "9-10", "11-13"))) |>
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_total_score = round(mean(standard_score, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            mean_percentile = round(mean(total_score, na.rm = TRUE), 1),
            .by = band) |>
  arrange(band)
```

The age bands make the point without any modelling: the variable labelled
`standard_score` rises monotonically across age while the one labelled
`total_score` does not.

### How age enters the model: three specifications

Age can enter these models in three defensible ways, and they answer different
questions.

| Spec | Specification | Question | Status in the manuscript |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | factor only, no age | baseline measurement model | Figures 7-8 |
| B | `factor ~ age` | how much factor variance is developmental | dropped (was used previously) |
| C | `indicator ~ age` for every indicator | does the factor cohere beyond shared age-related growth? | Table 8, age-controlled column |

B leaves age-driven covariance among the indicators intact, so it does not
test whether the factor is distinguishable from shared developmental growth.
C removes age from each indicator and estimates the factor from what remains.
Across an age range of 5 to 13 years this distinction is substantive.

```{r domain-age-specs}
#| dependson: domain-mefs-labels

build_age_specs <- function(factor_name, indicators) {
  measurement <- glue("{factor_name} =~ {paste(indicators, collapse = ' + ')}")
  list(
    `A no age`          = as.character(measurement),
    `B age -> factor`   = paste(measurement, glue("{factor_name} ~ age"), sep = "\n"),
    `C age -> indicators` = paste(measurement,
                                  paste(glue("{indicators} ~ age"), collapse = "\n"),
                                  sep = "\n")
  )
}

fit_domain <- function(syntax, data) {
  tryCatch(
    sem(syntax, data = data, estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml",
        std.lv = TRUE, optim.method = "nlminb",
        control = list(iter.max = 50000, rel.tol = 1e-6)),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
}

summarise_domain <- function(fits) {
  imap(fits, function(f, lab) {
    if (is.null(f) || !isTRUE(lavInspect(f, "converged")))
      return(tibble(spec = lab, note = "did not converge"))
    grab_measures(f, lab) |>
      dplyr::select(spec = model, df, chisq, cfi, rmsea, srmr) |>
      mutate(proper = isTRUE(suppressWarnings(lavInspect(f, "post.check"))))
  }) |> bind_rows()
}

loadings_domain <- function(fits) {
  imap(fits, function(f, lab) {
    if (is.null(f)) return(tibble())
    parameterEstimates(f, standardized = TRUE) |>
      filter(op == "=~") |>
      transmute(indicator = rhs, spec = lab, lambda = round(std.all, 3))
  }) |> bind_rows() |> pivot_wider(names_from = spec, values_from = lambda)
}

ef_indicators   <- c("hf", "mg", "sds", "mefs")
lang_indicators <- c("swr", "sre", "pa", "trog", "vocab")

ef_fits <- build_age_specs("EF", ef_indicators) |>
  map(\(syn) fit_domain(syn, ef_wide_scores))
lang_fits <- build_age_specs("Language", lang_indicators) |>
  map(\(syn) fit_domain(syn, lang_wide_scores))
```

### Diagrams for the three specifications

The three diagrams below show the same four (or five) tasks arranged the same
way each time: age on the left, the factor in the middle, the tasks on the
right. Only the arrows change.

- **Spec A** has no age at all. It asks: do these tasks hang together?
- **Spec B** has one arrow from age into the factor. It asks: how much of the
  factor is developmental?
- **Spec C** has an arrow from age into every task separately. It asks: do the
  tasks still hang together once each one's own age-related growth has been
  taken out?

The numbers on the arrows from the factor to each task are loadings: how
strongly that task reflects the factor, on a scale where 1 would be perfect.
Watch what happens to those numbers between B and C.

```{r domain-spec-diagrams}
#| results: "hide"

# The manuscript's plotting chunks are written for one model each, with node
# positions read from Excel. These specifications have different node sets
# (Spec A has no age) and different edges, so the layout is built in code here
# and the styling from `sem-ef-plot` is reused.
pretty_labels <- c(
  age = "Age\n(years)", EF = "Executive\nFunction", Language = "Language",
  hf = "Hearts and\nFlowers", mg = "Memory", sds = "Same and\nDifferent",
  mefs = "MEFS", swr = "ROAR\nWord", sre = "ROAR\nSentence",
  pa = "ROAR\nPhoneme", trog = "Sentence\nUnderstanding", vocab = "Vocabulary"
)

plot_domain_spec <- function(fit, factor_name, indicators) {
  nodes <- get_nodes(fit, columns = c("name", "shape")) |>
    mutate(label = coalesce(unname(pretty_labels[name]), name))

  edges <- parameterEstimates(fit, standardized = TRUE) |>
    filter(op %in% c("~", "=~", "~~")) |>
    transmute(
      lhs, rhs, op,
      from = if_else(op == "~", rhs, lhs),
      to   = if_else(op == "~", lhs, rhs),
      std.all, pvalue,
      arrow     = if_else(op == "~~" & lhs != rhs, "none",
                          if_else(op == "~~", "both", "last")),
      curvature = if_else(op == "~~" & lhs != rhs, 50, NA_real_),
      linetype  = if_else(op == "~~" & lhs != rhs, 2, 1),
      label = if_else(
        op %in% c("~", "=~"),
        sprintf("%.2f%s", std.all,
                case_when(pvalue < .001 ~ "***", pvalue < .01 ~ "**",
                          pvalue < .05 ~ "*", TRUE ~ "")),
        sprintf("%.2f", std.all))
    )

  # age left, factor centre, indicators right; blank column if age is absent
  has_age <- "age" %in% nodes$name
  # Indicators are spaced on alternate rows and the factor placed on a row
  # between them: if the factor sits level with an indicator it covers that
  # indicator's arrows and its loading label becomes unreadable.
  nr <- length(indicators) + 1
  mid <- ceiling(nr / 2)
  lay <- matrix("", nrow = nr, ncol = 3)
  lay[setdiff(seq_len(nr), mid), 3] <- indicators
  lay[mid, 2] <- factor_name
  if (has_age) lay[mid, 1] <- "age"
  lay <- lay[, colSums(lay != "") > 0, drop = FALSE]

  g <- tidySEM::prepare_graph(
    edges = edges, nodes = nodes, layout = lay,
    text_size = 3.2, rect_width = 7, rect_height = 3.5,
    ellipses_width = 7, ellipses_height = 3.5,
    variance_height = 2.5, variance_width = 2,
    arrow_angle = 15, arrow_length = .2,
    var_arrow_angle = 15, var_arrow_length = .1,
    spacing_y = 5, spacing_x = 7, fix_coord = FALSE
  )
  g$nodes$fill <- case_when(g$nodes$shape == "oval" ~ "#E8F2FF",
                            g$nodes$name == "age"   ~ "#FFF2E0",
                            TRUE ~ "#F5F5F5")
  g$nodes$colour <- "#1F1F1F"; g$nodes$font <- "#1F1F1F"
  g$edges$colour <- case_when(g$edges$op == "=~" ~ "#1B9E77",
                              g$edges$op == "~"  ~ "#386CB0",
                              TRUE ~ "#6B6B6B")
  g$edges$linetype <- if_else(g$edges$op == "~~", 2L, 1L)
  g$edges$size <- 0.6
  g$nodes$geom_text <- TRUE
  g$edges$label_fill <- "white"
  g$edges$label_colour <- "#1F1F1F"
  g$edges$label_alpha <- 1
  g
}
```

}

#| dependson: domain-age-specs

     "({sum(!is.na(ef_wide_scores$mefs))} with MEFS)")

summarise_domain(ef_fits) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

```

summarise_domain(lang_fits) |> mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

How much age variance each indicator carries, which determines how far its
loading moves between specifications:

```{r domain-age-per-indicator}
#| dependson: domain-age-specs

age_dependence <- function(data, indicators, domain) {
  map(indicators, function(v) {
    r <- cor(data[[v]], data$age, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
    tibble(domain = domain, indicator = v, r_age = r, r2_age = r^2)
  }) |> bind_rows()
}

bind_rows(
  age_dependence(ef_wide_scores, ef_indicators, "EF"),
  age_dependence(lang_wide_scores, lang_indicators, "Language")
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

Spec B is nested within spec C: B constrains age's association with each
indicator to operate entirely through the factor, which C leaves free. The
constraint is therefore testable.

```{r domain-b-vs-c}
#| dependson: domain-age-specs

compare_b_c <- function(fits, domain) {
  B <- fits[["B age -> factor"]]
  C <- fits[["C age -> indicators"]]
  if (is.null(B) || is.null(C)) return(tibble(domain = domain, note = "model missing"))
  lrt <- suppressWarnings(as.data.frame(lavTestLRT(B, C)))
  row <- lrt[!is.na(lrt[["Chisq diff"]]), ][1, ]
  tibble(
    domain = domain,
    df_B = fitMeasures(B)[["df"]], df_C = fitMeasures(C)[["df"]],
    chisq_diff = row[["Chisq diff"]], df_diff = row[["Df diff"]],
    p_value = row[["Pr(>Chisq)"]],
    aic_B = fitMeasures(B)[["aic"]], aic_C = fitMeasures(C)[["aic"]],
    bic_B = fitMeasures(B)[["bic"]], bic_C = fitMeasures(C)[["bic"]]
  )
}

bind_rows(compare_b_c(ef_fits, "EF"), compare_b_c(lang_fits, "Language")) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r domain-age-r2-factor}
#| dependson: domain-age-specs

# Proportion of factor variance attributable to age under spec B.
tibble(
  domain = c("EF", "Language"),
  r2_age_on_factor = c(
    lavInspect(ef_fits[["B age -> factor"]], "r2")[["EF"]],
    lavInspect(lang_fits[["B age -> factor"]], "r2")[["Language"]]
  )
) |> mutate(r2_age_on_factor = round(r2_age_on_factor, 3))
```

#### Interpretation

**Spec B's constraint is rejected for EF but not for Language.** For the EF
model, allowing age to predict each indicator directly improves fit by far more
than the three degrees of freedom it costs, and both information criteria
prefer spec C. For the Language model the constraint is not rejected, and BIC
prefers the more parsimonious spec B. Spec B was therefore adequate for
Language but not for EF, where age's association with the tasks does not
operate solely through the factor. This asymmetry is one reason the manuscript
now reports spec A alongside spec C for both domains rather than relying on
spec B for either: a specification that is defensible in one domain and
rejected in the other is a poor basis for a side-by-side validity claim.

**The EF factor depends heavily on age-related variance.** Under spec C the
Hearts and Flowers loading falls to a level at which it contributes little to
the factor, while Memory is retained and Same and Different is partly retained.
The movement tracks each indicator's age dependence: the two indicators
carrying the most age variance (Hearts and Flowers and MEFS) lose the most
between B and C, while Memory, which carries the least, becomes the dominant
indicator.
This is consistent with the observed partial correlations: controlling for age,
Hearts and Flowers correlates .03 with Same and Different and .11 with Memory,
whereas Memory and Same and Different correlate .39. A substantial part of what
the EF factor currently captures is shared age-related growth rather than a
common executive function dimension.

**The Language factor does not show this pattern.** All five loadings remain
strong under spec C, so Language coheres independently of age. This is not
because the Language indicators carry less age variance -- Word Reading
(r = .47) is as age-dependent as Hearts and Flowers (r = .47) -- but because
the Language tasks retain substantial shared variance once age is removed,
whereas Hearts and Flowers largely does not.

#### What these specifications license as claims

Two claims are available in principle: that the battery measures a
*developmental* construct, and that it measures *individual differences* in
that construct. The three specifications bear on them differently, and the two
domains come out differently.

**For Language, both claims hold.** Spec B is not rejected, so age's
association with the five tasks is adequately described as operating through a
common factor; that factor accounts for 31.5% of factor variance. All five
loadings remain strong under spec C, so the same factor also captures variation
among children of the same age. One model supports both readings.

**For EF, neither holds in unqualified form.** The rejection of spec B is
itself evidence against the developmental-construct reading: that reading
implies age acts on the tasks *through* a common dimension, which is the
constraint spec B imposes and the data reject. Age's associations with the four
tasks are task-specific. Separately, a correlation with age is weak evidence of
construct validity in any case -- most cognitive tasks show one, and the
age trends are already reported in `_05-age_models.qmd`. Construct validity is
a claim about covariance structure rather than about age slopes.

The individual-differences reading is partly supported for EF. Under spec C,
Memory, Same and Different, and MEFS retain substantial loadings, so a common
dimension does exist among children of the same age, and the MEFS loading
provides corroboration from an independent instrument rather than from internal
structure alone. Hearts and Flowers does not participate in that dimension.

The defensible statement for EF is therefore narrower than for Language:
Memory, Same and Different and MEFS share individual-difference variance beyond
age-related growth, supporting a common executive function dimension; Hearts
and Flowers does not contribute to it once age is controlled; and age's
associations with the tasks are task-specific rather than mediated by a single
factor.

Note also that the EF evidence leans on age more heavily than the Language
evidence does -- 39.9% of factor variance against 31.5%, combined with an
indicator that does not survive age partialling. These results are
specification comparisons on the same data, not evidence that any one
specification is correct.

### MEFS as a latent variable

In the manuscript, MEFS is an indicator of the same factor as the LEVANTE
tasks. That specification *assumes* convergent validity rather than estimating
it: the reported loading of .72 is MEFS's relation to a factor it helps define.

An alternative separates them, so that the quantity of interest is a
correlation between two constructs:

```
EF_levante =~ hf + mg + sds
MEFS_lat   =~ 1*mefs          # residual variance fixed from reliability
EF_levante ~~ MEFS_lat        # the validity coefficient
```

Because MEFS has a single indicator, its residual variance is not identified
and must be fixed. The task scores are standardised by `prep_sem()`, so the
residual variance is `1 - rxx` for an assumed reliability `rxx`.

**On the choice of `rxx`.** The MEFS Technical Report (2026, v. 07.26.26)
gives no internal
consistency estimate -- plausibly because the adaptive, accuracy-and-response-time
algorithm does not admit one -- and reports only test-retest ICCs, which vary by
sample, age range, device and delay: .93 (ages 2.5-5, same day, table-top), .95
(ages 2-5, table-top vs tablet), .92 (ages 3-15, two-week gap, NIH Toolbox
levels), .73 (ages 2+, 11-90 days, N = 2,034), and .86 / .85 / .85 / .71 / .70
by increasing delay (N = 333). None corresponds to the present sample, which is
ages 5-13, tablet-administered, and partly in Spanish and German outside the US
norming population.

Two further considerations argue against adopting any single value. The report
describes the .73 estimate as deflated, because those children were enrolled in
studies and programmes that may have acted as EF interventions. And test-retest
reliability is the wrong coefficient for this purpose: measured over an interval
it absorbs genuine developmental change as well as measurement error, so it
understates single-occasion reliability and over-corrects the correlation.

The analysis is therefore reported as a sensitivity range, with `rxx = 1`
(no correction) included as the reference case. That reference case is the
quantity that requires no assumption, and it is a lower bound.

```{r domain-mefs-latent}
#| dependson: domain-age-specs
#| cache: true

mefs_latent_fit <- function(rxx, with_age) {
  syntax <- glue(
    "EF_levante =~ 1*hf + mg + sds\n",
    "MEFS_lat =~ 1*mefs\n",
    "mefs ~~ {round(1 - rxx, 4)}*mefs\n",
    "EF_levante ~~ MEFS_lat",
    if (with_age) "\nEF_levante ~ age\nMEFS_lat ~ age" else ""
  )
  f <- tryCatch(
    sem(syntax, data = ef_wide_scores, estimator = "MLR", missing = "fiml",
        std.lv = FALSE, optim.method = "nlminb",
        control = list(iter.max = 50000, rel.tol = 1e-6)),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (is.null(f) || !isTRUE(lavInspect(f, "converged")))
    return(tibble(rxx = rxx, age = with_age, note = "did not converge"))

  r <- parameterEstimates(f, standardized = TRUE) |>
    filter(op == "~~", lhs == "EF_levante", rhs == "MEFS_lat") |>
    pull(std.all)

  tibble(rxx = rxx, age = with_age, r_EF_MEFS = r,
         cfi = fitMeasures(f)[["cfi"]], rmsea = fitMeasures(f)[["rmsea"]],
         proper = isTRUE(suppressWarnings(lavInspect(f, "post.check"))))
}

rxx_grid <- c(.70, .73, .80, .85, .90, .95, 1.00)

mefs_sensitivity <- expand_grid(rxx = rxx_grid, with_age = c(FALSE, TRUE)) |>
  pmap(\(rxx, with_age) mefs_latent_fit(rxx, with_age)) |>
  bind_rows()

# Fit is constant across rxx within each age condition (fixing a residual
# variance consumes no df), so it is reported separately rather than repeated.
mefs_sensitivity |>
  mutate(age = if_else(age, "age on both factors", "no age")) |>
  dplyr::select(rxx, age, r_EF_MEFS) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = age, values_from = r_EF_MEFS) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))

mefs_sensitivity |>
  summarise(cfi = first(cfi), rmsea = first(rmsea),
            all_proper = all(proper), .by = age) |>
  mutate(age = if_else(age, "age on both factors", "no age"),
         across(where(is.double), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

```{r domain-mefs-reference}
#| dependson: domain-mefs-latent

ref <- mefs_sensitivity |> filter(rxx == 1, !age)
rng <- mefs_sensitivity |> filter(!age) |> pull(r_EF_MEFS) |> range()

glue(
  "Reference case (no correction for MEFS unreliability): ",
  "r(EF_levante, MEFS) = {round(ref$r_EF_MEFS, 3)}. ",
  "Across assumed reliabilities of {min(rxx_grid)} to 1.00 the estimate ranges ",
  "from {round(rng[1], 3)} to {round(rng[2], 3)}."
)
```

#### Interpretation

Separating MEFS from the LEVANTE tasks yields a validity coefficient of about
.74 without any correction for MEFS's measurement error, which is slightly above
the .72 loading reported in the manuscript and requires no assumption about
reliability. Correcting for unreliability moves the estimate upward throughout,
reaching approximately .88 at the lowest reliability considered. The direction
is therefore unambiguous even though the magnitude is not: the uncorrected
estimate is a lower bound on the association between the LEVANTE executive
function construct and MEFS.

Fit is unaffected by `rxx`, since fixing a residual variance consumes no degrees
of freedom and the model-implied covariance structure among the observed
variables is unchanged.

Note that the models including age fit considerably worse than those without,
and give lower correlations throughout. This is the same pattern as spec B
versus spec C above: constraining age to act through the factors does not
describe these data well.
